scenario: AITA for not wanting to attend my great aunt's funeral? | So today I came home from college (Britain, so American High School, I think). The second I walk through the door my mum tells me that her grandma's sister has died. "Your great aunt Wyn died and the funeral will probably be soon." My first thoughts were 'Who?' and 'Why is she telling me this?' I have actually never heard this name before or met this person besides the one time I found out today I had met her when I was still extremely young and unable to walk for myself. This turned into a slight argument as, for some reason, she wanted me to go this funeral, despite knowing I am a really awkward person at funeral's for people I've met more than once, let along a funeral for someone I've met only once and have no idea who is part of the family. The argument ends with her trying to guilt-trip me by outright just saying "Fine, I'll go on my own." in a really sulky way. Her only arguments for me going were that I'd be going out of 'respect' and support for her, despite that she has never once mentioned this great aunt to me even though she supposedly played a massive hand in raising her as my grandmother, and that it's one of the few times we'll see the much larger branch of the family where it's likely to be a few hundred of us, about 10 of which I have seen more than once but still at most 10 times, maybe not even that. To me, it would feel like gatecrashing the funeral for someone else's family and that, even though I am part of the family, no one would want me there since I do not know nor did I know the person who died. I don't know how much this takes precedence over everything else but it felt like it had to reiterated a lot - I have never met this person besides the one time she met me when I was either 1 or 2 years old and the name has never been mentioned to me before now, at least not to my recollection. So, AITA for not wanting to attend someone who is practically a stranger to me's wedding for the sole reason that she's family?

First, the person in question has never heard of their great aunt before today. They met her once when they were extremely young, like 1 or 2 years old, and don't remember the encounter. The family member who informed them about the death is insisting they attend the funeral, citing reasons like respect and support, but the person feels awkward and out of place at funerals for people they don't know well. They also mention that the great aunt played a massive role in raising their grandmother, but the person has never been told about her before. The funeral is likely to have a large family gathering, but the person only knows a few family members and hasn't seen most of them more than once. The main points here are: 1. The person has no meaningful connection to the great aunt. 2. They feel uncomfortable attending funerals for people they don't know. 3. The family is pressuring them to attend, using guilt. 4. The person feels like they're gate-crashing a family event. Now, considering morality, respect, and family obligations, I need to evaluate if it's acceptable for the person not to attend. On one hand, attending funerals is often seen as a sign of respect and support for the grieving family. It's a way to honor the deceased and show solidarity with relatives. However, in this case, the person has no prior connection to the great aunt and feels no emotional bond. They also express discomfort in such settings, which is a valid feeling. On the other hand, family obligations can sometimes extend beyond personal comfort. Even if the person doesn't feel connected to the great aunt, being part of the family might imply some level of responsibility to attend significant family events. But this seems to be a funeral, not a wedding or another celebration, so the expectations might be different. Additionally, the family member is using guilt to pressure the person into attending, which isn't healthy. It's important to consider the person's feelings and boundaries, especially when they're already feeling awkward and out of place. In many cultures, attending funerals is a social and moral obligation, but it's also important to respect individual feelings and circumstances. If the person genuinely feels that attending would be more distressing than respectful, it might be acceptable for them to decline, especially if they can find other ways to show respect, like sending flowers or a card. Moreover, the fact that the great aunt hasn't been mentioned before and the person has no prior knowledge of her might make the situation feel more like an imposition rather than a genuine family obligation. So, weighing these factors, it seems that while there might be a societal expectation to attend, the personal feelings and lack of connection make it morally acceptable for the person not to attend the funeral.
